title: Lesson 6: Change Management Past the 30-Day On-Ramp
description: Change management past the 30-day on-ramp: why a month is too short for a behavior to become routine, the three post-on-ramp steps from Kotter's process (short-term wins, consolidate gains, anchor in culture), and how reinforcement and friction removal keep adoption alive.

questions.question: Why is treating the first month as the whole change effort a mistake?
options: People need at least a full year before any new behavior becomes an automatic routine
Habit research puts the median well past a month, so the effort must continue
Training sessions usually take longer than a month to schedule
Tools are typically replaced within a month of going live
questions.explanation: Automaticity takes far longer than a launch window, and the dip after the novelty fades is exactly when reinforcement matters most.

questions.question: After a pilot produces a clear win, what is the right next move?
options: Use the credibility from the win to extend the change into the next workflow
Declare success and hand the work back to the operating team to maintain on its own
Pause the program until the next budget cycle begins
Rerun the launch campaign to rebuild the earlier enthusiasm
questions.explanation: Declaring victory early lets old habits return, so a win should fund the next round of change rather than end the effort.

questions.question: What does it mean to anchor a new way of working?
options: Announcing the change at an all-hands meeting and in a company email
Assigning a champion to answer questions from peers
Writing the new way into documented process, onboarding, and review
Setting a target for how many people use the tool
questions.explanation: Anchoring makes the new behavior the default, written into process and expectations so it survives the people who started it.
